raw_case_text:
An 83-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital presenting with nausea, unsteadiness, and difficulties in walking. He had a two-month history of falls and abnormal gait. He had atrial fibrillation and was on acenocumarol (a vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant), and his family was concerned because of the risk of major bleeding after a fall. On physical examination, he had unsteady gait and dysdiadochokinesia. Eye-hand and eye-knee tests were abnormal. Cranial nerves and speech were normal, and the rest of the examination was unremarkable.
Anticoagulant therapy was discontinued due to the risk of a fall and major bleeding.
Routine laboratory data were normal, including kidney and liver panels. Haemoglobin, white blood cell count, and platelets were normal. A CT scan of the brain was performed, which did not show any acute abnormalities.
Over the days that followed, a gradual worsening occurred, with dysarthria, absent gag reflex and dysphagia, poor attention span, generalised hyperreflexia, and vertical nystagmus.
An MRI of the brain showed an asymmetric abnormal signal in both cerebellar peduncles, the cerebellar white matter, and the front area of the medulla (Figure 1). These abnormalities were hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with no gadolinium enhancement and no diffusion restriction. The right side structures were the most affected. The rest of the brain parenchyma was normal.
We consulted our neurologist to establish a differential diagnosis-based work-up. The abnormalities were not likely to be ischaemic or cancerous. However, inflammatory conditions, infectious diseases, primary central nervous system lymphoma, paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome, and demyelinating diseases should be ruled out.
Serologic tests including toxoplasma, HIV, CMV, and herpes simplex were negative. Immunological tests such as C3 and C4, immunoglobulin levels, and lymphocyte subsets were also normal. Tumour markers CA19.9, CEA, CA125, and PSA were normal. An abdominal ultrasound and a thoracic-abdominal CT scan did not reveal any abnormalities. A lumbar puncture was performed and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) revealed a glucose level of 110 mg/dl, proteins 42 mg/dl (normal range: 15-45 mg/dl), and leucocytes 1/mul. No oligoclonal bands were found.
While performing the work-up, two weeks after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated, with worsening of the neurological symptoms. He was lethargic and stuporous, with pauses in breathing. He started on steroid pulse therapy (1 g methylprednisolone daily for 5 days), but with no improvement.
A sample of the CSF was sent to a specialised laboratory in order to assess antineuronal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, and anti-Ri), which were negative. PCR for neurotropic viruses were also performed, and the JC virus PCR was positive in the CSF. The finding of the JC virus was reported the same day the patient passed away, three weeks after admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old male presented with nausea, unsteadiness, and gait difficulty superimposed on a 2-month history of recurrent falls and abnormal gait.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months prior to hospital admission, the patient experienced recurrent falls and progressive gait instability, culminating in acute nausea, unsteadiness, and difficulty walking. Over the days and weeks following admission, he progressively deteriorated with dysarthria, dysphagia, absent gag reflex, poor attention, vertical nystagmus, lethargy, stupor, and apneic spells.
subjective.past_medical_history: Atrial fibrillation maintained on acenocoumarol oral anticoagulation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, gait instability, falls, and subsequent inpatient dysarthria and dysphagia. Home medication: acenocoumarol (discontinued on admission due to fall/bleeding risk).

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological examination showed an unsteady ataxic gait, dysdiadochokinesia, and abnormal finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin coordination with intact cranial nerves and speech. Over the subsequent 2 weeks, examination evolved to show dysarthria, absent gag reflex, dysphagia, impaired attention, generalized hyperreflexia, vertical nystagmus, and progressive stupor with respiratory pauses.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, renal, and hepatic panels were normal. Serologies for Toxoplasma, HIV, CMV, and HSV were negative. Serum C3, C4, quantitative immunoglobulins, and tumor markers (CA19-9, CEA, CA125, PSA) were normal. Abdominal ultrasound was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets were normal. Initial head CT and thoracoabdominal CT were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated asymmetric T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense lesions without gadolinium enhancement or diffusion restriction involving both cerebellar peduncles (right greater than left), cerebellar white matter, and the anterior medulla. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed glucose 110 mg/dL, protein 42 mg/dL (normal 15–45 mg/dL), 1 leukocyte/µL, absent oligoclonal bands, negative paraneoplastic antineuronal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-Ri), and positive CSF JC virus PCR.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Posterior fossa / brainstem-cerebellar progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in an HIV-negative, apparently immunocompetent 83-year-old male (confirmed by positive CSF JC virus PCR and characteristic non-enhancing T2-hyperintense/T1-hypointense cerebellar peduncle and medullary white matter lesions on MRI, with normal lymphocyte subsets and negative HIV, autoimmune, and paraneoplastic panels). A 5-day pulse of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily) failed to halt his rapid bulbar and neurological decline, and the patient died 3 weeks after admission on the same day the positive CSF JC virus PCR result was reported.
